Thursday, October 29, 2026
More than 100 University of Chicago students, faculty and staff rallied in the Main Quad Wednesday night to protest the way the school has handled reports of sexual assault. The city is launching a new program to bring childhood lead testing directly to the South Side. The Chicago Bears have pulled off a blockbuster trade with the Tennessee Titans for star defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons. Plus, parents in Chicago have a wide range of choices when it comes to where their children go to school, but navigating the public school system can be daunting. Candidates for school board president have distinct views on how to help parents choose a school.
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
Wednesday, October 28, 2026
Election officials say early voting numbers in Chicago are up. Former Democratic Illinois Governor Pat Quinn is asking voters to check yes on a Cook County ballot referendum asking whether there should be a 3% income tax on millionaires. Voters in west suburban Oak Park are being asked what they think about Illinois fiscal policy. Plus, most low-income residents in Chicago who use housing vouchers to subsidize their rent live in high-poverty communities. That’s because there’s not enough affordable housing in low-poverty neighborhoods. Some landlords discriminate against renters using vouchers despite it being against the law. There is one tool that has helped thousands of people successfully move to higher-income neighborhoods and suburbs. They’re known as housing mobility programs.
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
Tuesday, October 27, 2026
The fall ballot will ask Chicago voters if they want a permanent site for large-scale festivals and events. Some homeowners on Chicago’s South and West sides could be eligible for thousands of dollars to help avoid losing their homes. Illinois Republican congressman Darin LaHood is asking the Trump administration to reconsider denying disaster aid to communities affected by severe weather in August. Plus, new analysis of more than two decades of travel times by WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times show gridlock on the Kennedy Expressway has never been worse than these past few years. We look into why record-breaking delays persist on the Kennedy.

articles.title: The Rundown: The Chicago area’s haunted history
articles.text:
The Rundown: The Chicago area’s haunted history - WBEZ Chicago
The watch towers at the Old Joliet Prison on Woodruff Road and Collins Street in Joliet, Illinois.
Manuel Martinez/WBEZ
The Rundown: WBEZ’s Daily Newsletter
The Rundown: The Chicago area’s haunted history
Plus, trapping an antimatter particle in a lab. Here’s what you need to know today.
By
Bianca Cseke
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Good afternoon! It’s Friday, and I’m over hearing “Monster Mash” and “Thriller” on repeat at every spooky season event — so I’m grateful for this playlist from my colleagues. Here’s what you need to know today.
1. These Chicago spots might just be haunted for real
Ahead of Halloween weekend, let’s take a look back at some scary tales WBEZ has collected over the years. You can read or listen to the full stories in the links. (But don’t blame me if you need to sleep with the lights on tonight.)
First stop: the Old Joliet Prison, where visitors say they’ve seen figures moving around in empty cells, captured photos of a woman in white floating in the prison yard and felt something grab them. Tour guide Larry Arroyo said he has witnessed many inexplicable things that seemed to be tied to some disturbing historical event. Spirits can exist, he believes, because of an unresolved matter or an injustice in a person’s death. That raises a question: Old Joliet Prison pops up on a lot of haunted lists, but do ghost stories detract from the specter of a truly dark history? [ WBEZ] [ Spotify]
Then there’s northwest suburban Barrington, which has about 10,000 residents — and contains only slightly fewer ghost stories. The town’s past includes mysterious accidents, desecrated graves, sketchy safe houses and the burned torso of a Mafia “stool pigeon.” Locals going about their business on the Northwest Highway near Cuba Road are driving the same stretch where Baby Face Nelson, on his way home to Barrington in 1934, got into a bloody machine-gun battle that took his life and the lives of two FBI agents. [ WBEZ] [ Spotify]
In Chicago’s Lake View neighborhood sits The Brewster, a 19th-century building best known as the home of Chucky, the doll who terrorized a family in the iconic horror film series “Child’s Play.” But before the movie, the site was considered haunted after the developer died from falling through the 8-story atrium; people have described sensations of falling. [ WBEZ]
WBEZ’s Curious City recently hosted a live event called “Tales from the Curious Crypt” at the Empty Bottle in Ukrainian Village. Storyteller Jonathan Pitts told an eerie tale of working late nights at the Athenaeum Center in Lake View, Vocalo’s Nudia Hernandez talked about a ghost that haunted her family’s home and Lily Be shared how her things were vanishing during a particularly difficult time in her life. [ WBEZ] [ Spotify]
Chicago is one of the most haunted cities in America (currently rated No. 3 by Travel & Leisure), meaning there’s no way I can fit all our city’s ghost stories in this summary. You can see or hear about more spooky spots in the links. [ Chicago Sun-Times] [ Spotify]
2. Billions of gallons of raw sewage is pouring into the Chicago River after storms
The Bridgeport Art Center sits along the South Branch of the Chicago River at a spot known as Bubbly Creek, a small body of water that marks the South Fork of the river and divides Bridgeport and McKinley Park.
This spot is disgusting after big storms, my colleague Brett Chase reports. Layers of feces, condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float past and get stuck in the low-lying trees along the shoreline. There are so many condoms that they’ve picked up a nickname: “Chicago whitefish.” Joe Gamble, who works at the Chicago Maritime Museum, said the smell sometimes clings to his clothes even after he’s left the area.
The culprit: a sewage pumping station on Racine Avenue south of the Bridgeport Art Center building. The big pumps help move sewer water — both wastewater and stormwater — to a treatment facility where it’s sanitized and sent to the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, then the Des Plaines and Illinois rivers and ultimately to the Mississippi River down to the Gulf of Mexico.
But sometimes, says the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, the government body that operates the station, heavy rains mean it needs to dump untreated sewage directly into the river to prevent flooding of homes. This year, the Racine station has dumped more than 10 billion gallons of sewage into the river — more than it has since 2019. In Chicago, stormwater and wastewater go into one big sewer.
Besides the ick factor, the sewage also poses a health risk for people with weak immune systems, because of the bacteria and other pathogens the water carries. The contaminated water also can wreak havoc on nature, wiping out fish populations for weeks. [ Chicago Sun-Times]
3. Housing mobility programs help low-income renters move up
As WBEZ’s Esther Yoon-Ji Kang reports, the court-ordered Gautreaux Assisted Housing Program is meant to address racial segregation in Chicago by helping low-income residents move to lower-crime, higher-income neighborhoods and suburbs.
The program originated from a 1966 lawsuit against the Chicago Housing Authority and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in which residents alleged the government intentionally placed Black families in segregated communities. The courts sided with the residents and ordered agencies to provide housing vouchers so families could move to mixed-income areas, often suburban, predominantly white or racially integrated neighborhoods. The program provided residents with housing-search counseling, landlord outreach and other resources.
Gautreaux is considered the country’s first housing mobility program, with The New York Times calling it a modern-day “underground railroad.” The success of the Gautreaux progr

articles.text:
What to know about the 2026 Illinois State Report Card and how schools in Chicago fared on key metrics - WBEZ Chicago
Illinois’ latest report card released Friday shows a larger portion of Chicago schools are considered to be in the state’s highest-ranked performance category.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times file
Education
Chicago School Board
What to know about the 2026 Illinois State Report Card and how schools in Chicago fared on key metrics
Parents may notice significant changes in the state report card this year, specifically how schools’ performance are categorized after the Illinois State Board of Education revamped its accountability system.
By
Makiya Seminera, Chalkbeat Chicago
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
After the Illinois State Board of Education changed the parameters for how it measures school-level performance earlier this year, the number of public schools in the state that are considered Exemplary — the state’s highest of five ratings — rose 17%
States are required by federal law to have an accountability system monitoring how schools perform on certain metrics. Under the previous system, only the top 10% of public schools in the state could achieve Exemplary status. Officials said that led to a lopsided distribution of schools stuck in the Commendable category — formerly the second-highest category. Now, 27% are considered Exemplary.
A new trove of data annually released as the Illinois Report Card also shows an uptick in the percentage of students considered proficient in reading and math. Roughly 56% of students are considered proficient in English language arts, while almost 40% are in math. That’s up from 53% and 38.5%, respectively.
Years prior to 2025 cannot be compared because last year, the state lowered the scores needed to be deemed proficient in English language arts and math.
Illinois school leaders and Chicago are touting record-high graduation rates. The state recorded a four-year graduation rate of nearly 89%, a little less than a one percentage point increase from last year. In CPS, graduation rates also saw positive movement after increasing for the second consecutive year from 82.5% in 2025 to more than 83% in 2026.
“The fact that we’re seeing the progress we are on a number of fronts is good news,” said Robin Steans, president of education advocacy group Advance Illinois.
The number of teachers in Illinois also continues to expand, now at nearly 144,000. Class sizes are generally trending downward, and the teacher retention rate is over 90% for the first time in over a decade. But teacher attendance rates are a cause for concern after they took a hit from the pandemic. In 2019, most Illinois teachers had high attendance — with 73% missing fewer than 10 days of school. Now, about 65% of teachers are in that category.
Here are three trends worth diving into from this year’s latest state report card data.
New state rating system opens door to exemplary status
One of the biggest differences families may notice about this year’s data is the new way Illinois categorizes public schools’ performance.
Instead of weighing schools against each other, schools are placed in one of five groups — Exemplary, Approaching Exemplary, Commendable, Developing, and Comprehensive — based on what the state calls core and elevating indicators.
“If you were a school district that had significant improvement from one year to the next, you could still be outperformed by another school and be kicked out of the Exemplary band, because only 10% of schools could be labeled as Exemplary under our old system,” Illinois State Superintendent of Education Tony Sanders said.
Although the categories aren’t exactly the same, the distribution of schools across the performance spectrum has shifted. Instead of labeling only the top 10% Exemplary, 27% of Illinois schools have earned the label. Last year, almost three-quarters of all Illinois public schools fell in the Commendable category, but with the introduction of a new second-highest ranking — Approaching Exemplary — Commendable schools make up a little more than a quarter of the total.
More Chicago schools are being considered Exemplary, with an increase from 2% of CPS schools in 2025 to 9% in 2026. The portion of schools in the bottom two rungs of the new ranking ladder also swelled compared to last year, when approximately 14% of CPS schools were in the two lowest categories. But CPS serves more students with higher needs, such as English learners and those from low income families.
The designations are helpful for assessing the state of student needs across the district, but they aren’t the end-all be-all, CPS deputy chief education officer Annise Lewis said. Internally, CPS no longer uses its old rating system that assigned schools letter or number grades after the teachers union’s pushback that it disproportionately penalized schools that served more high-needs students. Under the district’s current strategic plan, academic outcomes share importance with other goals such as student growth and well-being, Lewis said.
Proficiency trends up after Illinois cut score change
All public school students in grades 3-8 take the Illinois Assessment of Readiness. Students’ performance on the exam falls into one of four categories: above proficient, proficient, approaching proficient, and below proficient.
The state education board voted unanimously to lower the cut scores for the assessment in 2025, citing the need to match student abilities and reduce one of the highest cut scores in the nation. Several states had already lowered them after pandemic-related academic declines. The change means that state test scores diverge from a national test known as the Nation’s Report Card.

New from our Arts & Culture desk: the Green Room video podcast, which brings you closer to cultural conversations happening in Chicago and beyond. You can find it on YouTube, and we’ll keep our newsletter readers posted when there are new episodes.
Green Room Newsletter
You’re subscribed!
Please check your inbox for your confirmation.
Stay ahead of what’s hitting Chicago stages, galleries, museums and more with Green Room, WBEZ’s weekly arts & culture newsletter!
Sorry, there was an error registering your email.
Our first topic isn’t skimpy by any means: It’s about the withering state of expert criticism. Call it changes to technology, shorter attention spans or dwindling budgets at legacy media organizations: We’re staring down the barrel of a long, intractable shift in the world of expert opinion.
In 2025 alone, the culture desk at the New York Times reassigned four of its critics to new roles, the Chicago Tribune eliminated its film critic position and, in our own newsroom, the Chicago Sun-Times offered acclaimed film critic Richard Roeper a buyout. But criticism has been deteriorating even before the TikTok age: A 2021 Pew Research study found that newsroom employment across the country has fallen by over a quarter since 2008, impacting the job prospects of columnists and critics.
Is all hope lost for expert opinions? We gathered WBEZ theater reporter and critic Mike Davis, food reporter and critic Maggie Hennessy and film critic Reggie Ponder to discuss the ever-changing media landscape, the role of critics and what the pros can learn from influencers.
Have any thoughts about the state of criticism? Or want to let us know what you would like to hear from us in our next episode? Send us a note at arts@wbez.org or leave a comment on YouTube.

Whether you’re headed to a costume party or you’re passing out candy, Vocalo’s playlist will get you in the Halloween spirit.
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times

Arts & Culture
Vocalo brewed up this year’s witchiest Halloween playlist. Press play and start the party
If you’ve already listened to “Monster Mash” and “Thriller” too many times this October, we’ve got you covered.
By

What’s scarier than your Halloween costumes? Trying to make sure everyone is enjoying the music at your costume party. If you’re at a loss for a playlist, look no further.
The Vocalo team — plus some colleagues at WBEZ and the Sun-Times — put together two-plus hours of music, with no “Monster Mash,” “Ghostbusters,” “Time Warp” or “Thriller” in sight. Dance along to less overplayed on-theme songs like “Vamp Anthem” by Playboi Carti, “Dracula” by Tame Impala and “Witchy” by KAYTRANADA and Childish Gambino.
Give some love to other classics including Warren Zevon’s “Werewolves of London,” “Psycho Killer” by the Talking Heads and Ministry’s “Every Day Is Halloween.” Plus, check out horror film originals like 21 Savage’s “Spiral,” unofficially Halloween songs like “Heads Will Roll” by the Yeah Yeah Yeahs and others that just sound like the soundtrack to a themed party, like Nelly Furtado’s “Maneater.”
Hit play while you’re getting your costume on, in the car on the way to your Halloween plans or when your friend puts you on music duty at the party.

articles.title: Housing mobility programs help low-income renters move on up
articles.text:
Housing mobility programs help low-income renters move on up - WBEZ Chicago
Gloria Washington stands on the balcony of her apartment in Schaumburg. Washington moved from Chicago’s South Side to the northwest suburb in 1985 through a housing mobility program.
Esther Yoon-Ji Kang/WBEZ
Housing

Housing mobility programs help low-income renters move on up
Research shows moving low-income families to higher-income areas helps lift them out of poverty. But these mobility programs are costly. The Chicago Housing Authority runs the only one in Illinois.
By
Esther Yoon-Ji Kang
Updated
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
In 1985, Gloria Washington was living in a subsidized apartment in Chicago’s Englewood neighborhood. She says it was infested with rats and roaches, and there were always people drinking and doing drugs outside the building.
“I didn’t want that life for my two little kids,” recalled Washington, now 70.
She heard from her cousin about the Gautreaux Assisted Housing Program, a court-ordered program meant to address racial segregation in Chicago that helped low-income residents move to lower-crime, higher-income neighborhoods and suburbs.
When she was offered an apartment in the far northwest suburbs, she immediately said “yes.”
Washington remembered hearing that she would be moving to Schaumburg. At the time, she had only heard of the village on TV ads for a Schaumburg auto dealership.
“I said, ‘Why are they moving me to a car dealing place?’ ” Washington said. “But I just went along with the flow. I just wanted to get out of what situation I was in.”
Soon, she moved into a brand new, three-bedroom apartment with her young daughter and son. Despite loving her new digs, Washington was nervous about the lack of sidewalks. She had no car and no job, lived away from family, and sometimes got racist comments from people while walking places with her children.
But Washington also had help from the local township to pay bills. She was able to send her young son to daycare at Harper College, free of charge, while she attended classes there. The Pace suburban Bus’ Dial-A-Ride service also proved an invaluable tool for getting around. She found a job at a factory, got her associate degree, and then started working with adults with intellectual disabilities.
And the schools for her children, Washington said, were top-notch.
“[My kids] went to a nice high school with kids whose parents are judges and lawyers and doctors,” she said.
More than 40 years after she moved to Schaumburg, Washington still lives there. She’s now in a one-bedroom apartment just a few miles away from where she raised her kids. Both are grown and successful, living in nearby suburbs, she said.
Washington is one of thousands of people who moved from high-poverty Chicago neighborhoods to various suburbs and other parts of the city through the Gautreaux program in the 1980s and ’90s. The program originated from a 1966 lawsuit against the Chicago Housing Authority and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in which residents alleged that the government intentionally placed Black families in segregated communities.
The courts sided with the residents and ordered agencies to provide housing vouchers so families could move to mixed-income areas, often suburban, predominantly white or racially integrated neighborhoods. The program provided residents with housing search counseling, landlord outreach and other resources.
Gautreaux is considered the country’s first housing mobility program, with the New York Times calling it a modern-day “Underground Railroad” for helping low-income Black residents escape segregation in Chicago and move to suburban areas with more jobs, better schools and safer streets. The success of the Gautreaux program — which ended when it reached its court-ordered target of moving 7,100 families — helped spawn new housing mobility experiments throughout the country.
But today, as the city faces a housing crisis and many low-income voucher holders still live in segregated communities — some under substandard conditions — there is only one mobility program in Illinois. Researchers and housing advocates say while these programs are costly, they are effective in helping families — especially those with young children — rise out of poverty, and that more resources are needed from the federal government.
An aerial view of the Schaumburg municipal water tower. More than 40 years ago, through the Gautreaux Assisted Housing Program, Gloria Washington and her two young children moved to northwest suburban Schaumburg. Washington said the move changed her life and the lives of her children.
Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times
40 years of evidence
For decades, researchers have studied the effects of neighborhoods on families like Gloria Washington’s. Data from the Gautreaux program and subsequent housing mobility experiments throughout the country have consistently shown that residents moving from high-poverty, high-crime areas to lower-poverty, lower-crime neighborhoods — often referred to as “opportunity areas” — yield positive impacts on metrics like improved mental health and children’s outcomes.
“We have now almost 40 years of evidence that converges on this fact: It’s not only the family that a child is born into, but the neighborhood she grows up in that shapes her economic fortunes over time,” said Stefanie DeLuca, a professor at Johns Hopkins University and a researcher at Opportunity Insights, a nonpartisan think tank focused on economic mobility.
DeLuca has studied housing vouchers and residential mobility for decades.
“We can’t expect any one policy to do everything, but it’s remarkable what this policy is capable of,” she says.
In Chicago, about 40,000 households have CHA housing choice vouchers with which they rent apartments from private landlords. Most of those voucher holders live in majority-Black neighborhoods

articles.title: Billions of gallons of raw sewage are pouring into the Chicago River after storms

Billions of gallons of raw sewage are pouring into the Chicago River after storms - WBEZ Chicago
An aerial view of Bubbly Creek, the south fork of the south branch of the Chicago River.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
Environment
Billions of gallons of raw sewage are pouring into the Chicago River after storms
The massive, still-unfinished Deep Tunnel project was supposed to be the answer. But wastewater dumped in the river now threatens human health and wildlife. Here’s why — and some ideas on what can be done.
By
Brett Chase
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]

Print
Joe Gamble knows what to expect when he arrives at work at the Bridgeport Art Center after days of heavy rain.
“There was raw sewage floating in the creek,” Gamble says after storms in early October. “The wind carried the smell for at least a block or two.”
The Bridgeport Art Center sits along the south branch of the Chicago River at a spot known as Bubbly Creek, a small body of water that marks the south fork of the river and divides Bridgeport and McKinley Park.
It’s a really disgusting spot after big storms.
Layers of feces, condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float past and get stuck in the low-lying trees along the shoreline. There are so many condoms that they’ve picked up a nickname: “Chicago whitefish.”
More and more people have been drawn to the river in recent years for recreation, many of them taking to the water in canoes and kayaks.
Bubbly Creek appeals particularly to beginner rowers and paddlers because it’s calm and easy to navigate. After storms, though, it often stinks so badly that the smell clings to Gamble’s clothes even after he’s left the area.
“I am sometimes tolerant of smells,” says Gamble, who works at the Chicago Maritime Museum, “but it’s a different level.”
Joe Gamble works near Bubbly Creek. He says after a big storm it can stink so bad that the smell stays on his clothes even after he’s left the area.
Anthony Vazquez / Sun-Times
The culprit behind the stench? A sewage pumping station on Racine Avenue south of the Bridgeport Art Center building. The Racine Avenue pumping station has big pumps that help move sewer water — both wastewater and stormwater — to a treatment facility where it’s sanitized, then sent on to the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, then the Des Plaines and Illinois rivers and ultimately to the Mississippi River down to the Gulf of Mexico.
But sometimes the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, the government body that operates the station, says heavy rains mean it needs to dump untreated sewage directly into the river to prevent flooding of homes.
And it’s a lot of sewage. This year, the Racine station, which is nearly 90 years old, has dumped more than 10 billion gallons of sewage into the river. That’s more than it has since 2019. In Chicago, stormwater and wastewater go into one big sewer.
Like what happens at the Racine station on the South Side, the water reclamation district’s North Branch pumping station — at Lawrence Avenue and the river on the North Side, on the border of Albany Park and Lincoln Square — has spewed nearly 2 billion gallons of untreated sewage this year into the north branch of the Chicago River.
And all of this is happening despite the billions of dollars in taxpayer money that has been spent over 50 years on the Deep Tunnel project, the sprawling system of more than 100 miles of underground tunnels and massive reservoirs designed to capture floodwater in the Chicago area and help protect the river and Lake Michigan from pollution.
The Deep Tunnel is one of the many ways that government officials in Chicago and engineers have tried to adapt a big city that originally was built on a swamp and remains highly prone to flooding to its environment.
But climate change has complicated those efforts. It’s contributing to intensifying weather patterns that bring storms that drop rain faster and harder than ever before. That overwhelms our sewers, streets and homes.
These intense storms can bring us more than 8½ inches of rain in just 24 hours.
But Chicago’s sewer system, designed decades ago, can handle just 2 inches of rain before flooding is likely.
All of that sewage flowing into Bubbly Creek and the north branch of the river isn’t just gross. It also poses a health risk for people with weak immune systems because of the bacteria and other pathogens the water carries. The contaminated water also can wreak havoc with nature, wiping out fish populations for weeks. That’s bad for the larger ecosystem, something that environmental advocates and government officials have been working over the last three decades to restore.
Tara Hoffmann, executive director of Recovery on Water, a group that has a rowing team for breast cancer survivors, says she worries about keeping its members safe in the sometimes nasty water. Some of the women have compromised immune systems following their cancer treatment. And they are out on the water, rowing, much of the time during warm weather months.
Hoffmann recalls a particularly bad day on the creek in June, when the women were paddling through excrement.
“One of the first things you notice,” she says, “is fish up at the surface, gasping for air. They’re just desperate to breathe.”
Condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float atop the water and get stuck in low-lying trees along the Chicago River shoreline.
Anthony Vazquez / Sun-Times
A threat to wildlife
Both the Racine and North Branch pumping stations are owned by the water reclamation district. Since 2011, the independent government body that’s in charge of treating sewage and reducing flooding around Chicago has operated under a binding agreement with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over federal clean water violations related to the sewage.
District officials say the more intense storms we’re seeing mean that Chicago needs more flood prevention m
